strengths: MSAM addresses SAM’s computational cost with a simple implementation that reuses momentum and requires one gradient evaluation per step. Reported normalized speed of 0.99 versus SAM’s 0.52 supports its practical value.

Experiments cover several CNNs and ViTs on CIFAR100 and ImageNet, include relevant efficient-SAM baselines, and demonstrate compatibility with adaptive and BatchNorm-only perturbations. On CIFAR100 with WRN-16-4, MSAM reaches 79.11% versus SGD’s 76.90% and SAM’s 79.25%.

The negative-momentum observations and ablations on normalization, perturbation scheduling, and alternative directions provide useful insights connecting NAG and SAM. The appendix also includes meaningful comparisons under equal computational budgets.

The core algorithm is clearly presented, code and configurations are linked, and training settings and hyperparameter sweeps are documented. Instability and weaker results are acknowledged openly. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification in Appendix A.1 is invalid as stated. Proposition 1 fails for negative Hessian trace: with scalar Hessian -1, standard Gaussian perturbations, and rho=1, its left side is approximately -0.199 while the claimed upper bound is -1. Setting 1 does not impose nonnegative trace. Theorem 3 also leaves necessary population-loss smoothing assumptions and control of the Taylor remainder unstated. Consequently, the claim that improved generalization directly follows from this analysis is unsupported.

The ImageNet comparison uses different warm-up protocols despite evidence that the difference matters. MSAM’s perturbations are disabled during warm-up, whereas SAM’s remain active. Table A.2 shows that disabling SAM during warm-up improves its accuracy from 69.2% to 69.8%, exceeding MSAM’s 69.1%. The principal comparisons should incorporate this stronger SAM configuration.

Appendix A.15 reports the best perturbation strengths from extensive test-accuracy sweeps without specifying an independent validation-based selection protocol, leaving potential test-set selection bias unresolved. Most ImageNet results also use single runs; variability measured on smaller baseline models does not establish uncertainty for MSAM, particularly given its reported instability.

SAM-comparable accuracy is not consistently demonstrated on the harder configurations: MSAM obtains 75.8% versus SAM’s 78.2% for ViT-S/16 at 300 epochs, and 75.7% versus 77.7% for ViT-B/16. Equal-compute comparisons cover WRN-16-4 and ViT-S/32, leaving the tradeoff on these configurations unresolved. The theoretical and experimental-control gaps outweigh the promising efficiency results.
